warmup.q: You write the smallest Java program you can. It prints one line, hello, and exits. On Linux, about how many times does it ask the kernel for something before it's done?
options: Once: one request to print the line
About 100,000: once for every step the program takes
warmup.why: In this lesson's lab box, a Java hello world asks about 1,440 times. A program in the C language that prints the same line asks 28 times. Java code doesn't run on its own: it runs inside the JVM (Java Virtual Machine), a large program that must first set itself up. Most of its requests get memory and start about 20 threads, separate lines of work inside the program, which then wait for each other. The print itself is one request, called write. The last option is the trap for anyone who thinks a program needs the kernel for every step. Ordinary steps, such as adding two numbers, run straight on the processor and need no help.

sections.h: Many programs, one machine: why each one must ask the kernel
sections.html:
Right now your laptop runs dozens of programs on the same few processors, the same memory and the same disk. The processor, or CPU, is the chip that runs a program's instructions: tiny steps such as "add these two numbers". Memory (RAM) holds each program's working data while it runs, and the disk keeps files when the power is off.

Picture what happens if every program drove that hardware itself. The music player and a backup program write to the same spot on the disk at the same moment, and both files are ruined. A bug in a game writes over the memory where the chat app keeps your password. A program stuck in an endless loop keeps the processor forever, and nothing else ever runs again.

The first fix you might try is a shared library of careful code, with safe functions for the disk and memory. That doesn't help. Library code runs with exactly the powers of the program that called it, so a buggy or hostile program can skip the library and poke the hardware directly.

So the protection has to come from the processor itself. A CPU has two modes. In kernel mode it runs every instruction. In user mode it refuses the privileged ones, the instructions that talk to devices or change which memory a program can see. Code that tries one is stopped on the spot. arm64, the processor family in an Apple Silicon Mac, calls the two modes EL1 and EL0. x86-64, the family in most Windows laptops, calls them ring 0 and ring 3.

Now no program in user mode can hurt another, but it can't read a file either. It needs a controlled door, and a bank has the same problem. Customers can't walk into the vault. They fill in a slip, push it under the glass, and a teller checks it, does the work and slides back the result.

In a computer, the vault is the hardware and the teller is the kernel: the one program that runs in kernel mode. It owns the processors, the memory, the disks and the network card, and it decides which program runs next. Every other program runs in user mode: your browser, the shell where you type commands, even the JVM that runs Java code. A program that needs something fills in the slip, a system call: a request with a number that names the service. Examples are openat (open a file), read, write, mmap (give me memory) and clone (start a new line of work). The kernel checks the request, does the work and hands back a result. Linux has a few hundred of them, and on arm64, write is number 64.

The kernel also keeps a record for every program it runs: which memory is its own, which files it has open, who started it. A running program together with that record is a process. Lesson 2 of this track, Processes: fork, exec, wait and signals, opens the record.

The endless loop needs one more thing. Before the kernel lets a program run, it sets a timer in the hardware. In the lab box, the small Linux computer that Docker runs on your laptop for this track's Try its, the timer fires about every millisecond. Each time, the CPU stops the program and jumps into the kernel, which can pick another program to run. This is called a timer interrupt, and lesson 4, CPU scheduling, is about that choice.

The kernel and the programs that come with it, such as the shell and the basic tools, make up the operating system. The figure below is the picture for this whole track. Programs sit on top in user mode, the hardware at the bottom and the kernel in between, and system calls are the only door through. Each later lesson opens one box of the kernel. First, let's count how often a program knocks.

aside.title: Is Linux the kernel or the whole operating system?
aside.html: Strictly, Linux is only a kernel. Ubuntu, the system inside the lab box, is an operating system built around it: the Linux kernel plus a shell, the C library (code almost every program uses to make its system calls) and hundreds of tools such as ls. Android phones run the Linux kernel too, with very different programs on top. macOS and Windows each have a kernel of their own. So the details in this track are Linux's, but the picture of user mode, kernel mode and system calls holds for all of them.

sections.h: Counting the requests: 26 for doing nothing, 1,440 for Java
sections.html:
Let's watch the door. strace is a Linux tool that prints every system call a program makes, the way a camera over the bank counter would film every slip. It stops the program at each call, prints the call with its inputs and its result, and lets the program carry on. (It uses ptrace, the service the kernel offers to debugging tools.) Two options matter today. -c prints a count for each call instead of every line, and -f follows every thread and every new process the program starts. A thread is one line of work inside a program, with its own place in the code. A Java program runs many at once, and lesson 3 of this track looks at them closely.

Here is what three programs that do almost nothing ask for, counted in the lab box:

/bin/true                 26 system calls
C hello world             28
Java hello world       1,440

/bin/true is a program that does nothing at all and exits. It still needs 26 calls to start and stop. Most of them load the C library (libc), the code almost every Linux program uses to make its system calls, and set up memory. The C hello world, a few lines in the C language that print one line, adds one write and little else.

The Java program is another story. Java code doesn't run on the processor by itself. It runs inside the JVM, a large program that reads your code and carries it out. Before your main method starts, the JVM sets up three things. It makes a heap, the memory where your objects live, with a garbage collector that frees the objects nobody uses any more. It starts a JIT compiler, which turns code that runs often into fast instructions for the processor. And it starts about 20 threads to do all this work.

Each of those steps needs the kernel, and the top calls show it. mmap appears 275 times, to get memory for the heap and to load the JVM's own code. futex appears 258 times: one thread waiting for another, or waking it up. mprotect appears 219 times, to change what a piece of memory may be used for, such as "read only" or "may run as code". The one write that prints your line sits near the bottom of the list.

Remember your guess from the start? Over a thousand requests for one line of output is the cost of starting a whole JVM, and printing costs one. The Try it below gets you the same numbers. Next, let's follow that one write into the kernel.

try.title: Count system calls for three programs
steps: From the labs folder on your Mac, start the lab box: docker compose -f env/labbox.yml run --rm box. You land in a shell inside the box, in its /labs folder. strace works only on Linux. macOS has a similar tool, dtruss, but System Integrity Protection, the Mac's guard for its own system programs, blocks it for most programs. So run this track's Try its in the box.
Predict the totals for /bin/true, the C hello world and the Java one before you run anything.

Run the commands below. gcc turns the C program into a program you can run, and javac compiles the Java one. The first three strace -c lines print one total each, and the last line prints the JVM's top five calls and its total. The C program is os/c/l01/hello.c, and the Java one is os/src/demo/java/sfz/os/l01/demo/Hello.java.

code.title: in the lab box
code.html: strace -c /bin/true 2>&1 | tail -1 gcc -O2 -o /tmp/hello os/c/l01/hello.c strace -c /tmp/hello 2>&1 | tail -1 gcc -O2 -static -o /tmp/hello-static os/c/l01/hello.c strace -c /tmp/hello-static 2>&1 | tail -1 javac -d /tmp/out os/src/demo/java/sfz/os/l01/demo/*.java strace -f -c -S calls -o /tmp/jc.txt java -cp /tmp/out sfz.os.l01.demo.Hello 2>/dev/null head -7 /tmp/jc.txt; tail -1 /tmp/jc.txt

The third total is the same C program built with -static, which copies the C library into the program's own file. It needs no dynamic loader, the code that finds shared libraries such as libc.so.6 and loads them before main runs, so it makes half as many calls. Most entries in the errors column are normal. The loader and the JVM look for files in several places, and get ENOENT (no such file) until they find the right one.

sections.h: Following one request into the kernel and back
sections.html:
Asking the kernel can't be an ordinary function call. If a program could jump to any address in the kernel's code, it could land just past the part that checks permissions. Then it would run the rest with full power, like a customer who climbs over the counter.

So the CPU offers one special instruction that does three things at once. It switches to kernel mode. It saves where the program was. And it jumps to an entry point the kernel chose when the computer started up. The program can't choose where it lands. This switch is called a trap. On arm64 the instruction is svc (supervisor call), and the entry point is called the exception vector. On x86-64 the instruction is syscall.

With one door for everything, the kernel needs to be told which service you want, and with which inputs. Both travel in registers, the few dozen small storage slots inside the CPU that instructions work on directly. arm64 has 31 general ones, named x0 to x30. The service is a number, the system call number, like the form number printed on a bank slip. The kernel looks it up in its system call table to find the code that handles it.

Here is write(1, "ok\n", 3), which asks the kernel to write 3 bytes to file descriptor 1. A file descriptor is a small number a program uses to name something it has open, such as a file. 0 is standard input, 1 is standard output (usually your terminal window) and 2 is standard error, where error messages go.

  1. Your code calls the C library's write function. That part is an ordinary function call, still in user mode.
  2. The library's wrapper, a small function around the system call, puts the system call number, 64, in register x8, and the three inputs in x0, x1 and x2.
  3. It runs svc #0. The CPU traps: it saves the program counter (the address of the next instruction to run), switches from EL0 to EL1 and jumps to the kernel's entry point.
  4. The kernel reads x8, looks up entry 64 in its system call table and runs the code for write. That code checks that file descriptor 1 is open for writing, and copies the 3 bytes out of your program's memory.
  5. The kernel puts the result in x0 and runs eret (exception return), which switches back to user mode at the instruction right after svc.

Look again at step 4. The program hands over the buffer, the piece of memory that holds the bytes, as an address. A program could pass the address of the kernel's own memory as its "buffer", and ask the kernel to write the kernel's secrets to a file. So the kernel checks the address before it copies anything. An address from user mode could point anywhere. The kernel checks every one.

Errors come back as negative numbers. If a file is missing, openat puts -2 in x0. The C library turns that into a return value of -1. It also sets a variable called errno to 2, which has the name ENOENT (no such file or directory). strace shows both at once: = -1 ENOENT (No such file or directory). Java turns the same failure into a NoSuchFileException.

The bank picture breaks in two places. A teller takes minutes, and serves other people while you wait. A system call is far quicker, and the kernel does the work on your program's own processor, in time your program was already using.

How much quicker? In the lab box, one getpid system call (it asks "what's my process number?") takes about 150 ns, a nanosecond being a billionth of a second. That's nothing once and a lot a million times. A logger (the code that notes what a program did) that writes each line straight to its file, or a reader that pulls one byte at a time from the network, pays it on every piece. Next, we'll read a whole trace and see what the JVM asks for.

try.title: Watch a call succeed, then fail
steps: In the box, trace only the openat, read and write calls while cat, a program that prints files, prints one file that exists and one that doesn't.
Find the two openat lines, for /etc/hostname and /etc/nope. Compare what each one returned.

code.title: in the lab box
code.html: strace -e trace=openat,read,write cat /etc/hostname /etc/nope

try.expect:
strace's lines and cat's own output both go to the terminal, so they mix. Output trimmed to the interesting part:

openat(AT_FDCWD, "/etc/hostname", O_RDONLY) = 3
read(3, "box\n", 131072)                = 4
box
write(1, "box\n", 4)                    = 4
read(3, "", 131072)                     = 0
openat(AT_FDCWD, "/etc/nope", O_RDONLY) = -1 ENOENT (No such file or directory)
write(2, "cat: ", 5cat: )                    = 5
write(2, "/etc/nope", 9/etc/nope)                = 9
...
+++ exited with 1 +++

The first openat returns file descriptor 3, the small number that names the open file in the read calls after it. A read that returns 0 means the end of the file. The second openat returns -1 with ENOENT, so cat writes its complaint to file descriptor 2 (standard error) and exits with status 1, its way of saying something failed. There's no open call anywhere, because arm64 Linux only has openat. Guides written on x86-64 machines may show open, fork or stat. On arm64 you see openat, clone and newfstatat instead.

video.title: A system call crosses into the kernel

sections.h: Reading a trace: what the JVM asks for before your code runs
sections.html:
A count says how often. A full trace says what, and in which order. Here is the start of a full trace of the Java hello world. strace begins each line with a TID, a thread ID: the number the kernel gives each thread. These lines come from one run in the lab box (long lines trimmed):

143   execve("/opt/java/openjdk/bin/java", ["java", "-cp", "/tmp/out", "sfz.os.l01.demo.Hello"], 0xffffc2466180 /* 14 vars */) = 0
143   openat(AT_FDCWD, "/opt/java/openjdk/bin/libjli.so", O_RDONLY|O_CLOEXEC) = -1 ENOENT (No such file or directory)
143   openat(AT_FDCWD, "/opt/java/openjdk/bin/../lib/libjli.so", O_RDONLY|O_CLOEXEC) = 3
143   openat(AT_FDCWD, "/opt/java/openjdk/lib/server/libjvm.so", O_RDONLY|O_CLOEXEC) = 3
143   clone3({flags=CLONE_VM|CLONE_FS|CLONE_FILES|CLONE_SIGHAND|CLONE_THREAD|..., stack_size=0x1fca60, ...}, 88) = -1 ENOSYS (Function not implemented)
143   clone(child_stack=0xffff8a94ea60, flags=CLONE_VM|CLONE_FS|CLONE_FILES|CLONE_SIGHAND|CLONE_THREAD|..., parent_tid=[144], ...) = 144
143   futex(0xffff8a94f270, FUTEX_WAIT_BITSET|FUTEX_CLOCK_REALTIME, 144, NULL, FUTEX_BITSET_MATCH_ANY <unfinished ...>
144   write(1, "hello from the JVM\n", 19) = 19

execve loads a program into a process, here the java launcher: the small program that reads your command line and starts the JVM. The launcher needs two shared libraries, files of compiled code that a program loads when it starts (on Linux their names end in .so). It looks for libjli.so next to itself and gets ENOENT, then finds it one folder up, where openat returns 3, the file descriptor for the now-open file. (AT_FDCWD means "start from the current folder", and O_RDONLY means read only.) Then it opens libjvm.so, which is the JVM itself.

Then comes a surprise. The launcher doesn't run your program on its own thread. It starts thread 144 with clone, then waits on a futex until 144 is done. (A futex is the kernel's service for "let me sleep until this value changes". The 144 inside the call is the thread it waits for.) Thread 144 builds the JVM, and the JVM starts 19 more threads. Then 144 runs main and makes the one write that prints your line. The 19 include the garbage collector, the JIT compilers and a thread that handles signals, short messages the kernel delivers to a process, which lesson 2 explains. Thread 143, whose ID is also the process's ID, sits in that futex call until the end.

That surprise trips people up. Point strace at a running Java program without -f, and it watches only thread 143. You get one futex line and then silence, which looks like a program that's stuck. The other threads are busy, and strace isn't watching them. Add -f.

The failed clone3 line isn't a JVM bug either. clone3 is the newer way to start a thread, and glibc, the C library in the lab box, tries it first. The refusal comes from Docker. The lab box is a container, a group of programs that Docker keeps in a box of their own. Every container on a computer shares the one kernel underneath. So a bug in a rarely used system call, reachable from one container, would be a way into all of them.

Docker's answer is seccomp (secure computing), a filter the kernel runs on every system call a container makes, before the call itself runs. In the bank, it's a guard by the counter who turns away certain slips by their form number, before any teller sees them. Docker's default filter answers clone3 with ENOSYS, which means "this call doesn't exist". glibc believes it and falls back to the older clone, which does the same job.

The privileged lab box, box-priv, has no seccomp filter, and there all 20 threads start with clone3 on the first try. Same kernel, different guard. Next, we'll meet a few requests that never reach the door at all.

try.title: Find the JVM's threads in its trace
steps: In the box, save a full trace of the hello world to a file, then pull out the lines below. If this is a new box, run the javac line from the first Try it again first.
Count the clone( lines. Which thread wrote hello from the JVM: the one whose ID is the process ID, or another one?

Type exit to leave the box. Start the privileged box with docker compose -f env/labbox.yml run --rm box-priv, run javac -d /tmp/out os/src/demo/java/sfz/os/l01/demo/Hello.java, run the strace -f -o line again, then grep -c 'clone3(' /tmp/t.txt and grep -c 'clone(' /tmp/t.txt.

code.title: in the lab box
code.html: strace -f -o /tmp/t.txt java -cp /tmp/out sfz.os.l01.demo.Hello head -1 /tmp/t.txt grep clone3 /tmp/t.txt grep -c 'clone(' /tmp/t.txt grep 'write(1' /tmp/t.txt

try.expect:
Thread IDs change on every run. Long lines trimmed:

hello from the JVM
98    execve("/opt/java/openjdk/bin/java", ["java", "-cp", "/tmp/out", "sfz.os.l01.demo.Hello"], 0xffffda7a6fd0 /* 14 vars */) = 0
98    clone3({flags=CLONE_VM|CLONE_FS|CLONE_FILES|CLONE_SIGHAND|CLONE_THREAD|...}, 88) = -1 ENOSYS (Function not implemented)
20
99    write(1, "hello from the JVM\n", 19) = 19

One failed clone3, then 20 thread starts with clone. The line was written by thread 99, the one the launcher started, not by 98, whose ID is the process ID. In box-priv the two counts flip to 20 and 0: every thread starts with clone3, because no filter stands in the way.

sections.h: Requests that never reach the kernel: reading the clock
sections.html:
Programs read the clock all the time. In Java, System.nanoTime() returns a time in nanoseconds, and a café's payments program, which records each card payment, might call it twice per payment to time it. On Linux, reading a clock is the system call clock_gettime. At about 150 ns per trap, millions of reads add up to real processor time. Yet the time is only a number the kernel already knows, so a trip through the door to read it is a lot of ceremony.

The simplest fix: the kernel writes the current time into a page of memory that every process can read. A page is the unit the kernel hands out memory in, 4 KB in the lab box, and reading a number from memory takes a nanosecond or two. That version has two problems. The kernel updates the page while you might be reading it, so you could get half an old value and half a new one. And the raw value is a count of hardware clock ticks, which must be turned into nanoseconds with factors the kernel adjusts as it keeps the clock correct.

So the kernel places two things inside every process it starts: the data page, and a small piece of code that knows how to read it. The code checks a counter that the kernel bumps on every update, and reads again if an update was in progress. Then it turns the ticks into nanoseconds. Code plus data, already inside your process: that's the vDSO (virtual dynamic shared object), a shared library the kernel supplies itself. In the bank, it's the board on the wall with today's exchange rates. You read it yourself and never join the queue.

When you call clock_gettime, the C library calls the vDSO's version and never traps. On arm64 the vDSO offers three clock calls: clock_gettime, gettimeofday and clock_getres. It shows up in every process's memory map, the list of memory regions the process may use. /proc/self/maps prints that map, where the vDSO is two small regions: [vdso] for the code and [vvar] for the data.

The numbers from the lab box: a real system call (getpid) took about 150 ns, and a vDSO clock_gettime about 17 ns. A Java loop of one million System.nanoTime() calls ran at about 18 ns per call.

Two things follow. First, strace can't see vDSO calls, because they never reach the kernel. A trace of that million-call loop counts 3 clock_gettime system calls. All 3 come from the JVM's start-up, reading clocks that count how much processor time one thread has used, which the vDSO doesn't serve. If you trace a program to learn how often it reads the time, strace undercounts by a million. Second, seccomp can't filter those calls either, for the same reason: the guard only sees slips pushed under the glass.

So the payments program can time every payment with System.nanoTime() for tens of nanoseconds, without a single trap. The board only works for answers the kernel can post ahead of time, though. Reading a file, sending data over the network or starting a thread still needs a real system call. The rest of this track is about what the kernel does on the other side.

try.title: Time a trap, then watch the vDSO hide
steps: Predict: how many clock_gettime system calls will strace count for a loop that calls System.nanoTime() one million times?

Run the commands below in the box. os/c/l01/cost.c times one million getpid system calls against one million vDSO clock reads. NanoLoop is the Java loop. The last line prints the vDSO's two regions from the memory map.

code.title: in the lab box
code.html: gcc -O2 -o /tmp/cost os/c/l01/cost.c && /tmp/cost java -cp /tmp/out sfz.os.l01.demo.NanoLoop strace -f -c -e trace=clock_gettime java -cp /tmp/out sfz.os.l01.demo.NanoLoop 2>&1 | grep -v attached grep -E 'vdso|vvar' /proc/self/maps

try.expect:
getpid (system call):    151.0 ns per call
clock_gettime (vDSO):     16.9 ns per call
1,000,000 nanoTime() calls in 18 ms (18 ns each), checksum 1
1,000,000 nanoTime() calls in 19 ms (19 ns each), checksum 3
% time     seconds  usecs/call     calls    errors syscall
------ ----------- ----------- --------- --------- ----------------
  0.00    0.000000           0         3           clock_gettime
------ ----------- ----------- --------- --------- ----------------
100.00    0.000000           0         3           total
ffff9bd35000-ffff9bd37000 r--p 00000000 00:00 0                          [vvar]
ffff9bd37000-ffff9bd39000 r-xp 00000000 00:00 0                          [vdso]

A million clock reads, and strace counted 3 system calls. Your nanoseconds depend on your Mac's processor and on Docker, so expect different numbers. The gap of about 9 times between the two cost lines is what to look at. The addresses in the last two lines change on every run, because the kernel places the vDSO at a random address each time, which makes it harder for an attacker to find.

opening:
Picture your laptop on a busy afternoon. A browser with a dozen tabs, a music player and a chat app all run at once. They share one processor, one memory and one disk, yet none of them can see what another keeps in memory. When the browser freezes, the music keeps playing.

It's easy to think each program drives the machine itself: the music player reads the disk, and the chat app sends over the network. From inside the code, it looks that way. In Java, System.out.println("hello") looks like any other method call, and it returns almost at once. In fact, no program on your laptop can touch the disk, the screen or the network. Each one has to ask.

The networking track ended with the kernel, the core of the operating system, running every connection and timer for every program. In this lesson, we'll see why programs must ask the kernel for everything, count how often a tiny program asks, and follow one request in and back out. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a laptop where a dozen programs share one machine, and none can reach into another. The kernel keeps them apart. Every program runs in user mode, and each file, piece of memory or packet it wants is a system call. Even one line of Java asks about 1,400 times.

In the lab box, run strace -c ls / and read which calls a plain file listing needs. On a Mac, open Activity Monitor, the app that lists running programs, and look at how many processes your laptop runs right now.

Next, we'll open the kernel's record of a running program, and find out how a process is born, how it ends, and who hears about it.

compare.title: The same JVM start-up, with and without Docker's seccomp filter

a.label: box (Docker's default seccomp)
a.title: strace -f, lab box
a.html:
143   clone3({flags=CLONE_VM|CLONE_FS|CLONE_FILES|CLONE_SIGHAND|CLONE_THREAD|CLONE_SYSVSEM|CLONE_SETTLS|CLONE_PARENT_SETTID|CLONE_CHILD_CLEARTID, ...}, 88) = -1 ENOSYS (Function not implemented)
143   clone(child_stack=0xffff8a94ea60, flags=CLONE_VM|CLONE_FS|CLONE_FILES|CLONE_SIGHAND|CLONE_THREAD|CLONE_SYSVSEM|CLONE_SETTLS|CLONE_PARENT_SETTID|CLONE_CHILD_CLEARTID, parent_tid=[144], ...) = 144

$ grep -c 'clone3(' /tmp/t.txt
1
$ grep -c 'clone(' /tmp/t.txt
20

compare.note: Same kernel (Linux 6.12), same JDK (the Java Development Kit: the JVM and its tools), same program. In the default box, seccomp checks each call before the kernel runs it and answers clone3 with ENOSYS, so glibc tries again with clone. Docker does this on purpose. A seccomp filter can only look at the values in the call's registers. clone carries its settings, its flags, in a register, so the filter can check them and refuse the ones that would build the walls of a new container from inside this one. clone3 keeps its flags in memory, which the filter can't read, so Docker hides the call and lets glibc fall back. The answer has to be ENOSYS: glibc falls back only on that error, and any other answer would make every thread start fail.

worked.title: Read a JVM start-up from its trace

steps.say: You have /tmp/t.txt from strace -f -o. Start with its shape: how many threads appear in it, and how did the process begin? awk picks the first word of each line, the thread ID, and sort -u keeps one of each. These numbers come from the trace the lab uses, hello-jvm.strace.txt.
steps.code: # distinct thread IDs: the process plus every thread it started awk '{print $1}' /tmp/t.txt | sort -u | wc -l # 21 # how the process began head -1 /tmp/t.txt # 143 execve("/opt/java/openjdk/bin/java", ["java", "-cp", "/tmp/out", "sfz.os.l01.demo.Hello"], ...) = 0

steps.say: Next, group the failures by their error name. A healthy start-up has a long tail of failures, so learn what each one usually means before you call it a problem.
steps.code: grep -o '= -1 E[A-Z]*' /tmp/t.txt | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn # 29 = -1 EAGAIN # 23 = -1 ENOENT # 15 = -1 EINVAL # 3 = -1 ENOTTY # 1 = -1 ENOSYS # 1 = -1 EEXIST

steps.say: All 29 EAGAIN (try again) come from futex. A futex wait fails with EAGAIN when the value it waits on changed between the thread's check and the call, so it returns at once and lets the thread look again. ENOENT is the loader and the JVM looking for files. ENOTTY is a check for a terminal on something that isn't one. The single ENOSYS is the clone3 that seccomp refused.
steps.code: grep ENOSYS /tmp/t.txt | cut -c1-90 # 143 clone3({flags=CLONE_VM|CLONE_FS|CLONE_FILES|CLONE_SIGHAND|CLONE_THREAD|CLONE_SYSVSEM

steps.say: Last, the thread starts. A thread start is a clone or clone3 with CLONE_THREAD among its flags that returned a positive number, the new thread's ID. When another thread prints in the middle of a call, strace splits the call over two lines, marked <unfinished ...> and <... clone resumed>, so the result can sit far from the flags. A grep for = 145 would miss what it belongs to. That's why the lab builds a small parser, a program that reads the trace and joins the halves.

lab.title: Build an strace log analyzer
steps: Open hello-jvm.strace.txt. It's a real strace -f -o trace of this lesson's hello world, taken in the lab box. Find one line that ends in <unfinished ...>, and the resumed line that completes it.
Run the tests from the labs folder. All ten fail with NotImplementedError, because the code isn't written yet.

Write StraceParser.parseResult. Split the text on spaces. The first word is the result: ?, a hexadecimal number starting with 0x, or a plain decimal number. The second word is the error name, when it looks like E followed by capital letters.

Write StraceParser.parse. Match PREFIX to get the thread ID and the rest of the line. Try RESUMED, then UNFINISHED, then COMPLETE on the rest. Keep each unfinished half in a MutableMap<Int, Pair<String, String>> keyed by thread ID, and build the Syscall when its resumed half arrives.
Write the four StraceReport methods. Each one is a filter followed by a groupingBy or a map.
Run the tests until all ten pass. Then read what they check against the real trace: 1,453 calls, mmap the most common, 20 threads, one ENOSYS and 51 files opened.
hints: groupingBy { it.name }.eachCount() gives a Map<String, Int>. Sort its entries with sortedByDescending { it.value }, and rebuild the map with associate { it.key to it.value }, which keeps that order.
For hexadecimal, removePrefix("0x").toULong(16).toLong() handles every 64-bit value. Plain toLong(16) fails above Long.MAX_VALUE.
A clone without CLONE_THREAD creates a process, not a thread. That's what fork() does, as the next lesson shows. One test feeds you such a line from a tiny shell.
Regex("\"([^\"]*)\"").find(args) finds the first quoted string, which is the path in an openat call.

drill.title: The trap, from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lesson. Write down, in order, what happens from the moment your code calls write(1, buf, 3) until it gets 3 back. Name the processor's mode at each step, and the arm64 register that holds the system call number. Then compare with the answer.

answer.html:
1. user mode (EL0): your code calls libc write(), an ordinary function call
2. user mode: the wrapper puts 64 (write) in x8 and the arguments in x0, x1, x2
3. svc #0 traps: the CPU saves the user PC (program counter), switches
   EL0 -> EL1 and jumps to the kernel's entry point, the exception vector
4. kernel mode (EL1): look up entry 64 in the syscall table, run the write
   handler, check fd 1, copy 3 bytes from user memory
5. kernel mode: put the result in x0 (3, or a negative errno such as -9)
6. eret: back to EL0 at the instruction after svc
7. user mode: the wrapper returns 3 (or returns -1 and sets errno)

recap: Programs run in user mode, where the processor refuses the instructions that drive hardware. Only the kernel, in kernel mode, can touch the disks, the network card and other programs' memory.
A system call is a numbered request to the kernel. On arm64 the number goes in x8 and the inputs in x0 to x5, svc #0 traps into the kernel at a fixed entry point, and eret comes back.
A failed call returns a negative number. The C library turns it into -1 plus errno, and strace prints = -1 ENOENT (...).
A Java hello world makes about 1,440 system calls and starts 20 threads, almost all of them to set up the JVM. Trace Java with strace -f, or you watch only the launcher thread, which waits.
seccomp is a filter in front of the system calls. Docker's default filter answers clone3 with ENOSYS, so glibc falls back to clone.

The limit: the vDSO answers clock reads inside the process, in about 17 ns against about 150 ns for a trap, and strace and seccomp never see them. Everything else, from reading a file to starting a thread, pays for the trip into the kernel.

explain.prompt: A friend traced their program with strace -f -c for ten seconds. It showed 300,000 write calls but almost no clock_gettime, even though the code reads the clock for every request it handles. Explain both numbers in your own words, and say what you would change.
explain.answer: Every write is a system call. The processor traps into kernel mode, the kernel does the work and comes back, and that costs something like 150 ns each time. 300,000 writes in ten seconds is about one per log line, so the program writes each line on its own, with nothing collected in between. Collecting lines in memory and writing a few kilobytes at a time would cut the count 100 times or more. The clock reads are missing because clock_gettime goes through the vDSO, a small library the kernel places inside the process. It reads the time from a page of memory the kernel keeps up to date, in user mode, with no trap. strace only sees calls that enter the kernel, so it never counts them. They're cheap, so I'd leave them alone.

deeper.html:
Every container in the lab box runs behind a seccomp filter. You can see it in the process's status file, and you can watch it refuse a call:

$ grep Seccomp /proc/self/status
Seccomp:	2
Seccomp_filters:	1
$ unshare --user --map-root-user whoami
unshare: unshare failed: Operation not permitted
$ strace -f -e trace=unshare unshare --user --map-root-user whoami
unshare(CLONE_NEWUSER)                  = -1 EPERM (Operation not permitted)

Seccomp: 2 means filter mode. unshare(CLONE_NEWUSER) asks for a new user namespace: a private list of users, inside which this process may call itself root, the all-powerful user. Namespaces are a building block of containers, and lesson 12, Containers are processes: namespaces and cgroups, takes them apart. Docker's default filter refuses this call with EPERM (not permitted). In box-priv the same command prints root, and the status file says Seccomp: 0.

Docker's documentation says its default filter disables around 44 system calls out of more than 300. Most are calls a normal program never needs: loading new code into the kernel, changing the clock, rebooting, bpf and mount. The filter also hides the three io_uring calls, a newer and faster way to read and write, which lesson 11 comes back to. All containers on a computer share one kernel, so a kernel bug reachable from one container is a bug for every container. Fewer reachable calls means fewer chances.

A seccomp filter is a small BPF program, written in a simple language the kernel can check and run safely, that the kernel runs at the trap, before the system call table. It sees the call number, the processor family, the address of the instruction and the six input registers, and nothing else. It can't follow an address into memory. That's why it can't read clone3's flags, or the path given to openat. It's also why seccomp is good for "this program never needs mount" and useless for "this program may only open files under /data". Rules about paths need a different tool, such as AppArmor or SELinux, two Linux security systems that check names and paths.

One more number from this lesson to keep: the static C hello world made 14 system calls and the normal one 28. Half the work of a tiny program is the loader finding and loading libc.so.6. For a JVM, the loader's work is a rounding error next to libjvm.so building the heap and its threads.
